title: Messier 30, a stellar instructor
caption: The globular cluster Messier 30, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Messier 30, NGC 7099 · constellation Capricornus · about 27,500 light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, M. Libralato, G. Piotto, A. Sarajedini

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Month, November 2026 (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A bright, crowded ball of stars fills this Hubble view of Messier 30, a globular cluster about 27,500 light-years away in Capricornus. Charles Messier cataloged it among the fuzzy objects that could be mistaken for comets.

Globular clusters usually circle in a galaxy’s thin outer halo, much like insects around a light bulb. The Milky Way has at least 150, an estimated 11.5 to 13.5 billion years old. More than a century ago, Harlow Shapley used them to show that the Sun is not at our galaxy’s center, although his distances were off and he overestimated its size by about a factor of two.

Because they are so old, clusters born in the Milky Way are time capsules of the young galaxy. But not all of them were born here. M30 and many others move against the galaxy’s rotation, which may mean they were captured long ago.
scale: Using the source’s listed field of view (2.57 × 2.26 arcminutes) and its distance of about 27,500 light-years, the frame spans roughly 21 × 18 light-years. Its light set out about 27,500 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble’s cameras through five filters, from ultraviolet (275 nm) to near-infrared (814 nm). The color assigned to each filter isn’t published.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet and near-infrared light are invisible to the eye, and the colors are assigned, so the eye would not see this palette.

explore: Hubble has watched M30 for a long time. Its latest program measured how the cluster’s stars moved over 15 years, something only possible because of the telescope’s long life and sharp vision.
alt: A dense, glittering cluster of stars, brightest at its core, with scattered blue, white and red stars around it.
